architectural_implications.after: Organization-specific cloud harnesses own orchestration, isolation, and execution, replacing the local environment as the primary runtime.
architectural_implications.before: Local IDE plus a laptop was the seat of development; tooling was purchased or open-sourced and standardized.
architectural_implications.consequence: Harness design becomes an internal platform responsibility (sandboxing, secrets, resource scheduling, session state), and harness capability becomes a source of differentiation and lock-in.
architectural_implications.observation: Agentic harnesses are being built in-house by nearly every organization, and cloud agents are expected to displace local developer setups.

architectural_implications.after: Automated tests, evals, and formal verification carry the trust burden for designated non-critical paths; review persists only where risk justifies it.
architectural_implications.before: Human reviewer approval was the standard gate before merge for all code.
architectural_implications.consequence: The pipeline needs an explicit, enforceable classification of critical vs non-critical code, and the CI/CD layer must become the primary trust artifact — a significant shift in where assurance lives.
architectural_implications.observation: Code review responsibility is being removed for non-critical code rather than scaled.

architectural_implications.after: Agents are an entry point for work, with machine-originated PRs and issues competing with human-originated ones.
architectural_implications.before: Work originated in an IDE or ticket tracker with a human requester.
architectural_implications.consequence: Trigger surfaces, permissions, deduplication, and provenance tracking must be designed for non-human initiators; issue trackers and PR queues must handle machine-burst traffic.
architectural_implications.observation: Development initiates from chat (Slack bot tagging) and from production telemetry agents, not only from a developer's editor.

article_ideas.angle: Failure-mode analysis of the review bottleneck with a concrete migration path from human gate to automated gate, including the misclassification risk that becomes the new single point of failure.
article_ideas.audience: Staff+ engineers, platform/DevEx leads, engineering managers responsible for merge policy
article_ideas.thesis: A human review gate placed on an agent throughput path will always saturate and be bypassed, so the durable fix is to replace mandatory review with an enforceable, auditable automated gate (tests plus evals plus formal verification) paired with an explicit criticality rubric — not to add reviewers.
article_ideas.title: Zombie Reviews Are Not a Volume Problem: Why Agent-Era Code Review Needs an Automated Equivalent, Not a Headcount Increase

article_ideas.angle: Architecture argument that treats agent-originated PRs and issues as untrusted event streams, with concrete primitives for permissions, rate limits, and dedup.
article_ideas.based_on: perf-factory agents to monitor production and raise PRs
article_ideas.thesis: Once agents initiate work from production telemetry and Slack tags, the harness stops being a prompt router and becomes an event-driven actor system that requires admission control, idempotency, deduplication, provenance, and backpressure for machine-originated tasks.
article_ideas.title: The Agentic Software Factory Is an Event-Driven System: Design Admission Control Before You Auto-Merge Production PRs

article_ideas.angle: Risk-transfer argument: moving risk from reviewer attention to evaluation completeness makes eval design an explicit, auditable artifact and exposes unguarded production risk where evals are incomplete.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, test/eval infrastructure teams, quality-focused ICs
article_ideas.based_on: stop reading raw code and rely entirely on test validation

article_ideas.title: Code-Blind Engineering Shifts the Reliability Ceiling to Eval Coverage

article_ideas.angle: Capacity-planning argument for agent workloads: model cost and latency around the least elastic shared resource, and design harness architecture around where the real queue is.
article_ideas.audience: Infrastructure engineers, capacity planners, CTOs budgeting agent workloads
article_ideas.based_on: memory and CPU shortages in addition to GPUs

connections.relationship: Removing human review transfers the assurance burden to automated validation, making eval quality the new bottleneck.
Higher per-engineer concurrency increases PR volume, which is the same input that saturates the review pipeline.
Local hardware limits and capacity shortages are the stated drivers for moving agent execution to the cloud.
Perf-factory agents close the loop by turning production signals into self-initiated PRs.
Cheap execution raises the relative value of problem selection and influence over coding speed.

evidence_quotes.text: Traditional code reviews have become 'theater' or 'zombie code reviews' due to high volume, leading teams to phase them out for non-critical code.
Ramp and other startups phasing out code reviews for non-critical code.
Linear data showing agent-generated issues and PRs spiking past human-generated ones.

core_insights.generalization: Any human-in-the-loop gate placed on an agent throughput path will saturate and be bypassed rather than scaled; durable designs must replace the gate with an automated equivalent, not just increase reviewer headcount.
core_insights.insight: The code review pipeline is the first subsystem to structurally break under agent-generated volume: a 5x-10x spike in PRs/commits turns line-by-line human review into rubber-stamping ('zombie code reviews'), and the observed response is to remove mandatory review for non-critical code, shifting the trust burden onto automated tests, evals, and formal verification.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Review was the last human gate between generated code and production. If it is phased out by policy rather than replaced by an equivalent-strength automated gate, the safety of the whole delivery pipeline depends on how well evals, tests, and formal methods can substitute for human judgment.

evidence_quotes.text: Infrastructure capacity has strained, leading to memory and CPU shortages in addition to GPUs.
Cloud providers facing CPU back-ordering times up to 6 months.
Cloud agents and harnesses will replace local developer setups due to hardware limits and better cloud tooling.

core_insights.generalization: Scaling agent concurrency shifts the bottleneck to the least elastic shared resource, so harness architectures should be designed around where the real queue (CPU/memory provisioning) is, not the headline accelerator.
core_insights.insight: The binding compute constraint for AI-heavy engineering has drifted from GPUs to general-purpose infrastructure: memory and CPU shortages now appear alongside GPU scarcity, with cloud CPU back-order times of up to six months, which is what motivates moving agent workloads into the cloud instead of local machines.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Capacity planning and cost models for agentic workflows cannot assume GPU-only scarcity; sustained parallel agent sessions consume CPU/memory in ways that affect provisioning lead time, latency budgets, and the viability of local execution.

evidence_quotes.text: OpenAI's agentic software factory using perf-factory agents to monitor production and raise PRs.
Everyone is building their own AI coding harness/agent platform.
Development work frequently starts in Slack via bot tagging.

core_insights.generalization: Once agents can initiate work from their own signals, the harness needs admission control, provenance, and idempotency for machine-originated tasks, not just prompt routing.
core_insights.insight: The 'agentic software factory' pattern places autonomous agents on production telemetry: perf-factory agents monitor production and raise PRs themselves, making production observation an agent input rather than a human-only feedback loop, with development also frequently initiated by tagging a bot in Slack.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It moves agents from request-driven code generation to event-driven, always-on actors with their own trigger surface (telemetry, chat), which changes where you place permissions, rate limits, observability, and dedup/backpressure for self-initiated work.

evidence_quotes.text: Working with 5 to 10 parallel AI agents/worktrees is increasingly common among hardcore engineers.
Traditional heavy IDE usage is trending down as agentic interfaces like Codex, Antigravity, and Cursor take over.
Dima Zaychev running 5-10 worktrees locally to rotate between agents.

core_insights.generalization: Raising agent concurrency converts the human bottleneck from generation to orchestration and merge, so the harness must own isolation, session state, and conflict surfacing.
core_insights.insight: Parallelism is the new individual workflow unit: engineers run 5-10 concurrent agent sessions, typically isolated by worktrees (local) or cloud sessions, and are rotating between them rather than driving one task; heavy IDE usage declines as agentic interfaces become the primary surface.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Concurrency at the individual level requires isolation primitives (worktrees, sandboxes), context switching discipline, and per-session state; it also multiplies review/merge contention, which is why it interacts directly with the review bottleneck.

evidence_quotes.text: Anthropic migrating Zig to Rust in 11 days.
Asana migrating React testing libraries in 2 weeks.
Technical debt cleanup and large-scale refactoring are no longer multi-year boondoggles.

core_insights.generalization: Agent value concentrates where the task is voluminous, repetitive, and verifiable by tests — a criterion for choosing which work to hand to harnesses first.
core_insights.insight: Migrations that were multi-year projects collapse to days or weeks under agent harnesses — Anthropic's Zig-to-Rust migration in 11 days, Airbnb's Enzyme-to-RTL in 6 weeks, Asana's React testing library migration in 2 weeks — indicating agents are disproportionately effective on large, mechanical, well-specified refactors.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It identifies a concrete, high-leverage class of work (codemod-like, high-volume, spec-checkable transformation) where agent investment pays off first, and reframes technical debt cleanup as an economically tractable activity.

evidence_quotes.text: Engineers will stop reading raw code and rely entirely on test validation and agentic evaluations.
Jared Sumner noting that test writing ratio remains identical to pre-AI times.
Tests and validation are as important as ever to trust AI-generated code.

core_insights.generalization: Substituting automated validation for human inspection shifts risk from reviewer attention to evaluation completeness — an explicit, auditable artifact rather than tacit reviewer judgment.
core_insights.insight: The predicted endpoint is code-blind engineering: engineers stop reading raw code and rely entirely on test validation and agentic evaluations, while test-writing ratio reportedly stays the same as before AI — meaning validation effort is not reduced, only redistributed away from reading.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If reading is dropped, evals and tests become the sole specification of correctness, so their coverage, fidelity, and adversarial quality become the real reliability ceiling of the system; any gap in eval design becomes an unguarded production risk.

evidence_quotes.text: Engineers with deep domain knowledge (wisdom and charisma) are increasingly in-demand as intelligence becomes a commodity.
Titus Winters' framework on intelligence (how to do it), wisdom (what to do), and charisma (convincing others).
AI fluency and AI positivity are becoming baseline hiring requirements.

core_insights.generalization: When an execution capability becomes cheap, value migrates to the specification and adoption layers around it.
core_insights.insight: As code generation is commoditized, the scarce inputs become judgment and influence: Titus Winters' split of intelligence (how to do it), wisdom (what to do), and charisma (convincing others) is used to argue deep domain knowledge and persuasion outrank raw coding speed in hiring and value.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It implies engineering leverage shifts toward problem selection, intent specification, and cross-team alignment — the parts of the loop that agents cannot self-source — which changes what to measure and hire for.

project_ideas.name: Eval-Coverage Escape Benchmark
project_ideas.poc: Build a benchmark harness that runs identical agent-generated changes through two pipelines — one with human diff reading plus CI, one with CI plus agentic evals only — varying eval coverage and logging defect escapes with classification.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Gergely Orosz
  • Channel: The Pragmatic Engineer
  • Main topic: The state of the software engineering industry in 2026 driven by AI adoption, agentic workflows, and structural shifts in developer tooling and teams.
  • Purpose: To provide a comprehensive pragmatic overview of how AI adoption is transforming software engineering workflows, team structures, tools, and leadership in 2026. Gergely Orosz shares insights from visiting AI labs, Big Tech, and startups over recent months, examining what changed, what stayed the same, what broke, and what comes next in software engineering. Key changes include near-universal AI-generated code, parallel agent workflows, the fading relevance of traditional IDEs, agentic software factories, compressed migration timelines, and rising agent-generated issues. Unchanged aspects include teams and planning for complex work, testing and validation, and the need for human engineering judgment. Major system breaks include code review bottlenecks, infrastructure capacity shortages (CPU and memory), and increased cognitive load and burnout among engineers and leaders.

Topic Map

What Changed: AI Coding & Parallel Agents

  • Explanation: Software engineering has shifted to near 100% AI-generated code and parallel agent workflows where engineers run 5 to 10 agent sessions concurrently.
  • Key claims:
    • Nobody writes code by hand anymore except a few exceptions.
    • Working with 5 to 10 parallel AI agents/worktrees is increasingly common among hardcore engineers.
    • Traditional heavy IDE usage is trending down as agentic interfaces like Codex, Antigravity, and Cursor take over.
  • Examples:
    • Boris Cherry running 5 terminal tabs and 5-10 cloud code sessions in parallel.
    • Dima Zaychev running 5-10 worktrees locally to rotate between agents.
  • Terminology:
    • agentic harness
    • worktree
    • parallel agents
    • IDE
  • Why it matters: Engineers are no longer bottlenecked by typing speed or single-task limitations, multiplying output and cognitive overhead.

The Agentic Software Factory & Migrations

  • Explanation: Companies are building custom AI coding harnesses and agent platforms in-house, drastically accelerating codebases and migrations.
  • Key claims:
    • Everyone is building their own AI coding harness/agent platform.
    • Development work frequently starts in Slack via bot tagging.
    • Migrations that used to take years now take weeks or months (e.g., Anthropic Zig-to-Rust in 11 days, Airbnb Enzyme-to-RTL in 6 weeks).
  • Examples:
    • OpenAI's agentic software factory using perf-factory agents to monitor production and raise PRs.
    • Anthropic migrating Zig to Rust in 11 days.
    • Asana migrating React testing libraries in 2 weeks.
  • Terminology:
    • agentic software factory
    • perf-factory
    • agent-generated PRs
    • agent skills
  • Why it matters: Technical debt cleanup and large-scale refactoring are no longer multi-year boondoggles.

What Did Not Change

  • Explanation: Despite AI acceleration, fundamental engineering units, planning needs, and validation standards remain robust.
  • Key claims:
    • Teams are still the fundamental unit of work, retaining two-pizza team sizes.
    • Planning remains essential for complex infrastructure and alignment.
    • Tests and validation are as important as ever to trust AI-generated code.
    • Non-engineers are still not shipping production-ready code.
  • Examples:
    • Katelyn Less (Anthropic) emphasizing that two-pizza teams still exist despite human-agent collaboration.
    • Jared Sumner noting that test writing ratio remains identical to pre-AI times.
  • Terminology:
    • two-pizza team
    • formal verification
    • tracer bullets
  • Why it matters: Human accountability, collaboration, and rigorous validation cannot be automated away.

What Broke

  • Explanation: Massive increases in code quantity and agent activity broke traditional processes like code reviews, infrastructure capacity, and developer focus.
  • Key claims:
    • Code quantity and frequency assumptions have exploded (5x-10x increases in PRs and commits).
    • Traditional code reviews have become 'theater' or 'zombie code reviews' due to high volume, leading teams to phase them out for non-critical code.
    • Infrastructure capacity has strained, leading to memory and CPU shortages in addition to GPUs.
    • Engineering leadership is experiencing a wave of exits due to unrealistic expectations and founder mode pressures.
  • Examples:
    • Linear data showing agent-generated issues and PRs spiking past human-generated ones.
    • Ramp and other startups phasing out code reviews for non-critical code.
    • Cloud providers facing CPU back-ordering times up to 6 months.
  • Terminology:
    • zombie code reviews
    • CPU backlog
    • cognitive load
    • fractional CTO
  • Why it matters: Velocity gains create severe downstream system friction across review pipelines, hardware availability, and talent retention.

What Comes Next

  • Explanation: The industry is moving toward cloud agents, abandoning manual code reading, establishing agentic CI/CD infra, and valuing deep domain knowledge over raw coding speed.
  • Key claims:
    • Cloud agents and harnesses will replace local developer setups due to hardware limits and better cloud tooling.
    • Engineers will stop reading raw code and rely entirely on test validation and agentic evaluations.
    • AI fluency and AI positivity are becoming baseline hiring requirements.
    • Engineers with deep domain knowledge (wisdom and charisma) are increasingly in-demand as intelligence becomes a commodity.
  • Examples:
    • Ramp building advanced cloud agent harnesses.
    • Titus Winters' framework on intelligence (how to do it), wisdom (what to do), and charisma (convincing others).
  • Terminology:
    • cloud agents
    • AI fluency
    • deep domain knowledge
    • evals
  • Why it matters: The definition of a software engineer shifts from writing code to orchestrating systems, validating intent, and applying deep domain wisdom.

Key Points

Nobody writes code by hand anymore

  • Explanation: Virtually all software development involves AI generation and prompting, shifting human effort to reviewing, prompting, and orchestrating.
  • Evidence: Observed switch to near 100% AI-generated code in startups and tech companies since early 2025.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must master prompt engineering, multi-agent management, and system architecture rather than syntax.

Code reviews are breaking down

  • Explanation: The sheer volume of agent-generated code has turned code reviews into a rubber-stamping theater, prompting companies to eliminate mandatory reviews for non-critical code.
  • Evidence: Linear data showing massive spikes in agent PRs; startup policies shifting to trust-and-verify.
  • Practical implication: Automated testing, evaluation suites (evals), and formal verification must replace human line-by-line code review.

Wisdom and charisma outperform raw intelligence

  • Explanation: As code generation becomes free and instant, knowing what to build and why matters more than knowing how to code.
  • Evidence: Titus Winters' formula: intelligence is cheap, but wisdom and charisma are scarce and valuable.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must cultivate deep domain expertise, product sense, and leadership skills.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Titus Winters' Success Framework

  • How it works: Breaks down engineering capability into three pillars where intelligence is becoming a commodity and wisdom/charisma become paramount.
  • Components:
    • Intelligence (how to do it)
    • Wisdom (what to do)
    • Charisma (convince others to do it)
  • When to use: When evaluating career positioning and skill development in an AI-dominated engineering landscape.

Examples & Case Studies

Anthropic migrated from Zig to Rust in 11 days with a single engineer.

  • Illustrates: Massive acceleration of legacy migrations using AI agents.
  • Lesson: Refactoring and rewriting codebases is no longer cost-prohibitive or multi-year.

Linear data showing agent-generated tickets and PRs exceeding human-generated ones in mid-2026.

  • Illustrates: The emergence of the agentic software factory at scale.
  • Lesson: Issue trackers and PR pipelines must adapt to non-human contributors.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Adopt parallel agent workflows to multiply your output.
    • Integrate automated eval suites into CI/CD pipelines to replace broken human code reviews.
    • Embrace cloud-based development environments and harnesses.
  • Strategic:
    • Focus on deep domain knowledge and system design rather than syntax and implementation.

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Gergely Orosz
- **Channel**: The Pragmatic Engineer
- **Main topic**: The state of the software engineering industry in 2026 driven by AI adoption, agentic workflows, and structural shifts in developer tooling and teams.
- **Purpose**: To provide a comprehensive pragmatic overview of how AI adoption is transforming software engineering workflows, team structures, tools, and leadership in 2026.
Gergely Orosz shares insights from visiting AI labs, Big Tech, and startups over recent months, examining what changed, what stayed the same, what broke, and what comes next in software engineering. Key changes include near-universal AI-generated code, parallel agent workflows, the fading relevance of traditional IDEs, agentic software factories, compressed migration timelines, and rising agent-generated issues. Unchanged aspects include teams and planning for complex work, testing and validation, and the need for human engineering judgment. Major system breaks include code review bottlenecks, infrastructure capacity shortages (CPU and memory), and increased cognitive load and burnout among engineers and leaders.
## Topic Map
### What Changed: AI Coding & Parallel Agents
- **Explanation**: Software engineering has shifted to near 100% AI-generated code and parallel agent workflows where engineers run 5 to 10 agent sessions concurrently.
- **Key claims**:
  - Nobody writes code by hand anymore except a few exceptions.
  - Working with 5 to 10 parallel AI agents/worktrees is increasingly common among hardcore engineers.
  - Traditional heavy IDE usage is trending down as agentic interfaces like Codex, Antigravity, and Cursor take over.
- **Examples**:
  - Boris Cherry running 5 terminal tabs and 5-10 cloud code sessions in parallel.
  - Dima Zaychev running 5-10 worktrees locally to rotate between agents.
- **Terminology**:
  - agentic harness
  - worktree
  - parallel agents
  - IDE
- **Why it matters**: Engineers are no longer bottlenecked by typing speed or single-task limitations, multiplying output and cognitive overhead.
### The Agentic Software Factory & Migrations
- **Explanation**: Companies are building custom AI coding harnesses and agent platforms in-house, drastically accelerating codebases and migrations.
- **Key claims**:
  - Everyone is building their own AI coding harness/agent platform.
  - Development work frequently starts in Slack via bot tagging.
  - Migrations that used to take years now take weeks or months (e.g., Anthropic Zig-to-Rust in 11 days, Airbnb Enzyme-to-RTL in 6 weeks).
- **Examples**:
  - OpenAI's agentic software factory using perf-factory agents to monitor production and raise PRs.
  - Anthropic migrating Zig to Rust in 11 days.
  - Asana migrating React testing libraries in 2 weeks.
- **Terminology**:
  - agentic software factory
  - perf-factory
  - agent-generated PRs
  - agent skills
- **Why it matters**: Technical debt cleanup and large-scale refactoring are no longer multi-year boondoggles.
### What Did Not Change
- **Explanation**: Despite AI acceleration, fundamental engineering units, planning needs, and validation standards remain robust.
- **Key claims**:
  - Teams are still the fundamental unit of work, retaining two-pizza team sizes.
  - Planning remains essential for complex infrastructure and alignment.
  - Tests and validation are as important as ever to trust AI-generated code.
  - Non-engineers are still not shipping production-ready code.
- **Examples**:
  - Katelyn Less (Anthropic) emphasizing that two-pizza teams still exist despite human-agent collaboration.
  - Jared Sumner noting that test writing ratio remains identical to pre-AI times.
- **Terminology**:
  - two-pizza team
  - formal verification
  - tracer bullets
- **Why it matters**: Human accountability, collaboration, and rigorous validation cannot be automated away.
### What Broke
- **Explanation**: Massive increases in code quantity and agent activity broke traditional processes like code reviews, infrastructure capacity, and developer focus.
- **Key claims**:
  - Code quantity and frequency assumptions have exploded (5x-10x increases in PRs and commits).
  - Traditional code reviews have become 'theater' or 'zombie code reviews' due to high volume, leading teams to phase them out for non-critical code.
  - Infrastructure capacity has strained, leading to memory and CPU shortages in addition to GPUs.
  - Engineering leadership is experiencing a wave of exits due to unrealistic expectations and founder mode pressures.
- **Examples**:
  - Linear data showing agent-generated issues and PRs spiking past human-generated ones.
  - Ramp and other startups phasing out code reviews for non-critical code.
  - Cloud providers facing CPU back-ordering times up to 6 months.
- **Terminology**:
  - zombie code reviews
  - CPU backlog
  - cognitive load
  - fractional CTO
- **Why it matters**: Velocity gains create severe downstream system friction across review pipelines, hardware availability, and talent retention.
### What Comes Next
- **Explanation**: The industry is moving toward cloud agents, abandoning manual code reading, establishing agentic CI/CD infra, and valuing deep domain knowledge over raw coding speed.
- **Key claims**:
  - Cloud agents and harnesses will replace local developer setups due to hardware limits and better cloud tooling.
  - Engineers will stop reading raw code and rely entirely on test validation and agentic evaluations.
  - AI fluency and AI positivity are becoming baseline hiring requirements.
  - Engineers with deep domain knowledge (wisdom and charisma) are increasingly in-demand as intelligence becomes a commodity.
- **Examples**:
  - Ramp building advanced cloud agent harnesses.
  - Titus Winters' framework on intelligence (how to do it), wisdom (what to do), and charisma (convincing others).
- **Terminology**:
  - cloud agents
  - AI fluency
  - deep domain knowledge
  - evals
- **Why it matters**: The definition of a software engineer shifts from writing code to orchestrating systems, validating intent, and applying deep domain wisdom.
## Key Points
### Nobody writes code by hand anymore
- **Explanation**: Virtually all software development involves AI generation and prompting, shifting human effort to reviewing, prompting, and orchestrating.
- **Evidence**: Observed switch to near 100% AI-generated code in startups and tech companies since early 2025.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers must master prompt engineering, multi-agent management, and system architecture rather than syntax.
### Code reviews are breaking down
- **Explanation**: The sheer volume of agent-generated code has turned code reviews into a rubber-stamping theater, prompting companies to eliminate mandatory reviews for non-critical code.
- **Evidence**: Linear data showing massive spikes in agent PRs; startup policies shifting to trust-and-verify.
- **Practical implication**: Automated testing, evaluation suites (evals), and formal verification must replace human line-by-line code review.
### Wisdom and charisma outperform raw intelligence
- **Explanation**: As code generation becomes free and instant, knowing *what* to build and *why* matters more than knowing *how* to code.
- **Evidence**: Titus Winters' formula: intelligence is cheap, but wisdom and charisma are scarce and valuable.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers must cultivate deep domain expertise, product sense, and leadership skills.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Titus Winters' Success Framework
- **How it works**: Breaks down engineering capability into three pillars where intelligence is becoming a commodity and wisdom/charisma become paramount.
- **Components**:
  - Intelligence (how to do it)
  - Wisdom (what to do)
  - Charisma (convince others to do it)
- **When to use**: When evaluating career positioning and skill development in an AI-dominated engineering landscape.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Anthropic migrated from Zig to Rust in 11 days with a single engineer.
- **Illustrates**: Massive acceleration of legacy migrations using AI agents.
- **Lesson**: Refactoring and rewriting codebases is no longer cost-prohibitive or multi-year.
### Linear data showing agent-generated tickets and PRs exceeding human-generated ones in mid-2026.
- **Illustrates**: The emergence of the agentic software factory at scale.
- **Lesson**: Issue trackers and PR pipelines must adapt to non-human contributors.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Adopt parallel agent workflows to multiply your output.
  - Integrate automated eval suites into CI/CD pipelines to replace broken human code reviews.
  - Embrace cloud-based development environments and harnesses.
- **Strategic**:
